content: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic gastrointestinal condition that occurs worldwide and significantly contributes to illness and disability. It is typically categorized into two main types: Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). Helminths, which are parasitic worms with complex life cycles, can reside in tissues or the gastrointestinal lumen of their hosts, often causing long-lasting or chronic infections that are frequently asymptomatic. These parasites are known to modulate the immune responses of their hosts. Observational and experimental studies suggest that helminths may suppress immune-mediated chronic inflammation, which is characteristic of conditions such as asthma, allergies, and IBD. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of helminth therapy for inducing remission in patients with IBD. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and the Cochrane Inflammatory Bowel Disease Group Specialized Trials Register, up until July 13, 2013. Additional searches were performed in online trial registries and conference abstracts, with no restrictions on language. The inclusion criteria for the study were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that involved any species or combination of helminths, administered in any dose, route, or duration, to patients with active CD or UC. The diagnosis of these conditions was confirmed using clinical, endoscopic, or histological criteria. Data extraction and eligibility assessment were independently performed by two authors using a standardized form. Statistical analyses were conducted using RevMan software. The primary outcome was the induction of remission, as defined by the included studies. Secondary outcomes included clinical, histological, or endoscopic improvement, mucosal healing, changes in disease activity and quality of life scores, hospitalizations, need for intravenous corticosteroids or surgery, study withdrawals, and adverse events. Risk ratios (RR) and mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for dichotomous and continuous outcomes, respectively. The methodological quality of the studies was assessed using the Cochrane risk of bias tool, and the overall quality of evidence for each outcome was evaluated using the GRADE criteria. Two RCTs, involving a total of 90 participants, were included in the analysis. One trial investigated the efficacy and safety of Trichuris suis (T. suis) ova in patients with UC (n = 54), while the other was a phase 1 trial assessing the safety and tolerability of T. suis ova in patients with CD (n = 36). Both studies were judged to have a low risk of bias. In the UC study, participants in the treatment group received biweekly doses of 2,500 T. suis eggs suspended in 0.8 mL of saline over a 12-week period, while the placebo group received 0.8 mL of saline alone. Data on clinical remission and improvement were limited. In the T. suis group, 10% (3/30) of patients achieved clinical remission compared to 4% (1/24) in the placebo group (RR 2.40, 95% CI 0.27 to 21.63). Clinical improvement was observed in 43% (13/30) of patients in the T. suis group compared to 17% (4/24) in the placebo group (RR 2.60, 95% CI 0.97 to 6.95). The mean ulcerative colitis disease activity index (UCDAI) score was lower in the T. suis group (6.1 ± 0.61) compared to the placebo group (7.5 ± 0.66) after 12 weeks of treatment (MD -1.40, 95% CI -1.75 to -1.05). Adverse events were infrequent, with 3% (1/30) of patients in the T. suis group experiencing at least one adverse event compared to 12% (3/24) in the placebo group (RR 0.27, 95% CI 0.03 to 2.40). None of the reported adverse events were deemed related to the study treatment. The overall quality of evidence for clinical remission and improvement was rated as low due to serious imprecision. In the CD study, participants received a single dose of T. suis ova at varying concentrations: 500 (n = 9), 2,500 (n = 9), or 7,500 (n = 9) embryonated eggs, or a matching placebo (n = 9). This study did not evaluate clinical remission or improvement as outcomes. Adverse event data were limited to a two-week period. At least one adverse event was reported in 37% (10/27) of patients in the T. suis group compared to 44% (4/9) in the placebo group (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.35 to 2.01). Only one adverse event, dysgeusia (a distortion of taste), was considered possibly related to treatment, occurring in one patient in the T. suis group and one patient in the placebo group. In conclusion, the current evidence is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about the efficacy and safety of helminth therapy for IBD. The primary efficacy outcomes in this review are based on a single small study with low-quality evidence due to serious imprecision. There is also insufficient evidence to determine the safety of helminth therapy in patients with UC and CD. Further randomized controlled trials are necessary to evaluate the potential benefits and risks of helminth therapy in IBD.
